scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll emerged from swing dance traditions established around 1920 in the United States, evolving through Lindy Hop and Boogie-Woogie before crystallizing around 1955 alongside the music genre.
In France, Lyon became a major incubator for the sport in the late 1960s, where local practitioners structured the dance into a commercial and competitive discipline.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Acrobatic Rock'n'Roll is primarily performed in formal competitions, World Cups, and international championships regulated by the World Rock'N'Roll Confederation, functioning as a high-performance elite sports discipline.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced in pairs or groups, the form relies on precise 6-basic or 9-basic kick-ball-change footwork executed on the balls of the feet.
Competitors alternate between rapid floor choreography and regulated acrobatic maneuvers, including lifts, jumps, throws, and flips.
Watch for Einsteiger, Todessturz.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear progression across the competition floor or stationary placement during acrobatics

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to a 4/4 measure at very fast tempos between 176 and 208 beats per minute (46 to 52 bars per minute), emphasizing the first and third beats.
Modern tournaments favor high-tempo disco and pop music over traditional vintage recordings.
Listen for the synthesizers, electronic percussion, modern pop instrumentation.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 192 beats a minute.
Very fast modern pop and disco tracks with a heavy 4/4 driving rhythm, synthesized basslines, and punchy percussion designed to sustain rapid athletic movement.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Competitors wear form-fitting, multicoloured outfits made of elastic artificial fibres tailored individually to allow complete freedom of movement and prevent friction burns during acrobatics.
Footwear includes light jazz shoes for dance segments and aerobics sneakers for shock absorption during aerial landings.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Notable figures associated with the sport include French world champion Miguel Angueira, Katerina Tikhonova, and early French developers such as Jacques Bense and Bernard Farhi.
Specific rules, age categories, and allowed acrobatics vary by country and national association, though international standards are harmonized under WRRC safety levels.
Derived from Lindy Hop and Boogie-Woogie, evolving directly into modern competitive acrobatic rock and roll.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 is first steps. Today we learn the basic 6-step weight transfer.
The level is beginner. The difficulty of the dance overall is advanced.
Your instructor is a rigorous former competitive coach emphasizing precision and safety.
on_screen: Instructor front view, name of the chapter, the three things you will learn

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Keep an upright, tightly controlled core, dancing almost exclusively on the balls of the feet.
Use active arm movements coordinated with leg kicks at clear, regular angles.
Initiate partner lifts and throws with body wave movements.
on_screen: Instructor front then side view; freeze-frame on validated posture

scenes.title: Count and rhythm
narration: Count: 1-2-3-4 then 5-6-7-8 (eight counts, two bars). The meter is 4/4.
Rhythm pattern: Fast-paced offbeat phrasing with deliberate stress on the 1st and 3rd beats.
Clap it first, then step it in place.
on_screen: Counts on screen, flashing on the beat
Metronome at 134 bpm
scenes.music: lesson_slow (clicks only until the step lands)

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1 uses the 6-basic step.
Step 2 uses the 9-basic step with kick-ball-change.
Footwork follows the 6-basic and 9-basic kick-ball-change with sharp, linear kicks.
Drill this with step-step-kick-settle movements.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Practice ball of foot bouncing.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Combine Step A and Step B without stopping, starting slowly.
Progress to half tempo, then full tempo.
The instructor faces you in a mirror, so your right matches your right.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full
